title: Type Aliases and Union Types
summary: A type alias gives a type a name. A union says that a value can be one of several allowed types.
introduction: A type alias gives a type a name. A union says that a value can be one of several allowed types. Name a useful shape once so you can reuse it. Then describe a value that may be text or a number, and check it before using it.
learningObjectives: Create type aliases for primitives, unions, objects and function types
Explain why a union value only exposes the members shared by every alternative
Combine object types with an intersection and choose between type and interface

blocks.text: The `type` keyword gives a name to any type: a primitive, a union, an object shape, a function signature or a tuple. The alias is purely a name; it creates no new type and no runtime code. Aliases shine when the same union would otherwise be repeated in ten signatures.

blocks.title: alias.ts
npx tsc alias.ts
blocks.content:
alias.ts:10:25 - error TS2345: Argument of type '"huge"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Size'.

10 console.log(label("x2", "huge"));
                           ~~~~~~


Found 1 error in alias.ts:10

blocks.text: The first two calls print `7-small` and `x1-large`. The third is caught because `"huge"` is not one of the three literals in `Size`. A union of string literals is the lightest way to model a fixed set of options; the [enums lesson](/tutorials/typescript/enums-literals) compares it with `enum`.

A union says *one of these, but I do not know which*. The compiler therefore lets you use only what every member supports. `padStart` exists on strings but not on numbers, so calling it on a `string | number` is an error, and the message spells out which member lacks it.

blocks.title: pad.ts
npx tsc pad.ts
blocks.content:
pad.ts:2:16 - error TS2339: Property 'padStart' does not exist on type 'string | number'.
  Property 'padStart' does not exist on type 'number'.

2   return value.padStart(4, "0");
                 ~~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in pad.ts:2

blocks.text: The fix is to check which member you have. A `typeof` test narrows `value` to `number` inside the `if` and to `string` after it, so each branch can use the right methods. This is the core move of the [narrowing lesson](/tutorials/typescript/narrowing); here is the simplest form.

blocks.title: pad-fixed.ts

blocks.text: Where a union means *either*, an intersection (`&`) means *both*. Intersecting two object types produces a type that has every property of each, which is handy for mixing in shared fields such as timestamps. Aliases also work for function types and tuples, as `Handler` shows.

blocks.title: intersection.ts
npx tsc intersection.ts
blocks.content:
intersection.ts:17:7 - error TS2322: Type '"text"' is not assignable to type 'never'.

17 const nothing: Impossible = "text";
         ~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in intersection.ts:17

blocks.title: Common mistake: intersecting types that cannot overlap
blocks.text: `string & number` is not an error on the line that declares it. The compiler quietly reduces it to `never`, the type with no values, and the problem only surfaces later as `not assignable to type 'never'`. The same happens when two object types declare the same property with incompatible types. Intersections are for *combining* compatible shapes, not for narrowing; use a union plus a check for that.
For a plain object shape, the two are interchangeable, and consistency within a codebase matters more than the choice. The real differences are in what each one *can* do.

rows: No; a duplicate name is an error
Yes, when it is an object type

blocks.text: A practical rule: use `interface` for object shapes that other code will extend or implement, and `type` for everything else, especially unions. Angular, for instance, uses interfaces for component inputs and type aliases for state unions such as `"loading" | "ready" | "error"`.

blocks.title: Unions of objects
blocks.text: A union can also combine object types: `type Result = { ok: true; value: number } | { ok: false; error: string }`. The shared `ok` property with different literal types lets the compiler tell the members apart. This *discriminated union* pattern is one of the most useful ideas in TypeScript and gets its own section in the narrowing lesson.

questions.question: Which method can be called directly on a value of type `string | string[]` without narrowing?
questions.explanation: Only members that exist on every union member are available. Both strings and arrays have length and slice; toUpperCase exists only on strings and push only on arrays.

questions.question: A type alias can describe a union, but an interface cannot.
questions.explanation: Interfaces describe object shapes only. Unions, primitives, tuples and function types need the type keyword.
